Consultancy Project: 
Germany & Argentina 
By: Carson & Sophie S

●
Provides a basis or managers to 
reference their past experiences on 
in order to work in new countries
●
Helps managers to understand 
cultural differences before they 
start managing another team
●
A cheap yet effective tool 
international companies should 
invest in to strengthen their global 
capacity
Importance of Erin 
Meyer’s County 
Mapping

Overview on Differences
●
Communication is passionate, 
open, expressive, and opinionated 
●
Flexibility is common
○
Punctuality is appreciated, 
but isn’t expected
●
Strong emphasis on relationships 
and building them
●
Feedback should be given 
respectfully, otherwise it maybe 
taken personally
●
Structured, thoroughly planned 
out, focused on efﬁciency and order 
●
Strong emphasis on timelines and 
being punctual on deadlines 
●
Data driven mindset with an 
emphasis on procedure based 
methods 
●
Respect for a professional 
hierarchy 
German Work Culture
Argentinian Work Culture

Communicating
German managers should:
●
Resist the instinct to explicitly outline exact expectations
●
Rely more on face to face communication, get to know 
your employees 
●
Avoid being too direct, as it could come off as blunt or 
aggressive.
○
Argentinians do not require such direct 
expectations being communicated, as they 
are more used to interpreting expectations 
●
Actively listen to their employees and look out for indirect 
communication
○
Argentinian employees will likely express 
their concerns in an unspoken manner, 
which can be new to German managers.
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Communication is be passionate and open and 
statements are very opinionated and expressive
●
Direct input is very likely
●
Culture drives off of indirect communication (from 
nonverbal cues to gestures)
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Be direct when communicating and take control of 
the conversation 
●
Ensure communication is clear and to-the-point
●
Know that communication can be blunt
Argentina

Evaluating
German managers will be most successful and 
better received when they use strategic and kind 
language while evaluating their Argentinian 
counterparts.
German managers will likely have the instinct to 
be very blunt with their feedback, and while 
Argentinians will be receptive to receiving 
feedback from their superiors, they appreciate 
private settings, respectful tones, and 
constructive approaches. German managers 
should be cautious that their directness is not 
interpreted as disrespect.
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Feedback should be given carefully
●
Personal feelings are attached
●
Giving feedback with constructive feedback and 
clear context is important
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Not “sugar coat” feedback and be blunt
●
Outline in detail how this feedback is logical and 
detail-focused
●
Outline the beneﬁts when correcting behavior 
●
Celebrate regular performance milestone 
Argentina

Leading
●
Balance authority with collaboration 
○
authority & hierarchy will be respected, 
but collaboration is a sign of a strong 
leader
●
create and maintain relationships with 
Argentinian employees in which care and an 
interest in wellbeing is prioritized 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Hierarchy should be maintained
○
Managers should be approachable, present, 
interested, visible and engaged
●
One-on-one meetings and check-ins should be 
regular
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Should provide quality and excellence to their 
employees
●
Have clearly deﬁned relationships
●
Give precise directions so no questions need to be 
asked 
Argentina

Deciding
●
German managers should create speciﬁc 
timelines for their Argentinian employees to 
follow, and explain clearly and directly how 
their work will be used later on   
●
It's important to remember that Argentinian 
employees will likely expect clarity from their 
managers, so through decision making it 
would be beneﬁcial for managers to explain 
the reasoning behind their decisions 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Hierarchy matters (people of higher status do not 
collaborate with someone lower than them
●
Decisions are made on personal preference of the 
decision maker
●
Avoid high-pressure tactics that are confrontational
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Detail the process and the beneﬁts when making 
decisions
●
Understand that Germans will comply
●
Not be overly authoritarian
Argentina

Trusting
●
Argentinian trust is based in relationships 
building and personal expressions of informal 
communication and mutual respect 
●
German managers should do slightly against 
their instincts to build trust purely based off 
performance and data, but rather through 
casual meetings and check ins to show care 
and compassion beyond business stats 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Relationships matter heavily (gained through 
consistency and care)
●
Hierarchy ≠ trust
●
Nepotism is common -> higher levels of trust 
●
Averted to change
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Always be truthful with details
●
Understand that “no” means that they know they 
aren’t capable of performing the task
●
Show up on time to build good trust
Argentina

Disagreeing
●
Argentinian employees are more likely to take 
disagreements or confrontations personally, 
especially if they are not handled with respect 
●
hierarchy is a big value for Argentinians, so 
when their clearly outlined superior gives 
them constructive feedback or respectfully 
disagrees with them, it is likely to be received 
very well 
●
additionally, a sign of respect while 
disagreeing is to express concerns in private 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Ideas that are brought up should be treated carefully 
to protect the reputation of the participant
●
Avoid confrontation
○
Argentinians do not like publicly admitting 
they’re wrong
●
Disagreements can be subtle
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Be straightforward in disagreements
●
Understand that “no” is a normal answer
●
Know that leaders have the ultimate ﬁnal say
Argentina

Scheduling
●
German managers should speciﬁcally and 
thoughtfully frame deadlines and scheduling 
details in a clear way, as Argentinians may 
view timelines as suggestions or optional if 
not told otherwise
○
this could create a conﬂict as Germans 
are more likely to follow deadlines more 
speciﬁcally, and could mistakenly 
assume that Argentinians not following 
a timeline is not professional 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Appointments are made in advance, but are 
ﬂexible
●
Avoid scheduling meetings during peak months 
●
Arrive on time, even though the person you are 
meeting might not
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Arrive on time (“time is money”)
●
Understand deadlines strict
●
Assign extra work if deadlines are not complete
Argentina

Persuading
●
German work culture strongly values 
principles, so for a German manager they will 
likely persuade through logic and date 
●
A German manager should alter this way of 
thinking to a more personal approach of 
persuasion, in which real world tangible 
examples are shown and personal relevance 
is utilized, beyond just business. 
Germany
Culture in Argentina
●
Heavily linked to personal experiences
○
Due to the values and relationships that 
they build
●
They employ more applications-based approach, 
using past experiences 
Argentinian Managers Should
●
Apply more logic when persuading
●
Use facts and essential information
●
Not get caught cutting corners 
Argentina

Recommendations: Germany 
Here are some key recommendations for a German manager working in Argentina:
1.
Place logic slightly after personal relationships 
2.
Clarify authority in order to establish a healthy dynamic 
3.
Be sensitive while giving feedback and deliver negative feedback in private 
4.
Take the time to build and foster personal relationships

Recommendations: Argentina 
Here are some key recommendations for an Argentinian manager working in Germany
1.
Be very respectful to deadlines and do not try to push them
2.
Understand the importance of time 
3.
Ensure that all employees have all the materials they need to complete tasks (“no 
questions asked”)
4.
Lead with facts and precise details when talking with anyone
